cards.explanation: The answer is that her father will not let Samson enter. Samson, an Israelite, shows up at his wife's home and says, “I want to go to my wife in her room…” But her father would not let him enter (Judges 15:1). That door stays shut, friends. Whatever Samson pictured for this visit, I bet it didn't start with a closed door.

The answer is her younger sister. Her father asks, “Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she?” Then he says, “Please take her instead” (Judges 15:2). I think he's trying to make things right on the spot. Friends, it's like a bakery handing you a different batch when you came for the one you ordered.

The answer is that he will be blameless in doing it. Samson says, “This time I will be blameless in doing harm to the Philistines” (Judges 15:3). Later the men of Judah tell him the Philistines rule over them (Judges 15:11). Notice he says “this time.” I think he feels the door slammed in his face, and he's done being polite.

The answer is torch. Samson turns the foxes tail-to-tail and fastens a torch between each pair of tails (Judges 15:4). That's the whole setup. Three hundred foxes and all those torches is a lot of prep, friends.

The answer is into the Philistines' standing grain. Samson lit the torches and released the foxes into the standing grain of the Philistines (Judges 15:5). The grain was standing out in the fields, ready for harvest. That's where the fire starts. And that is a very bad day for a harvest.

The answer is False. The fire burned up the piles of grain and the standing grain, as well as the vineyards and olive groves (Judges 15:5). It didn't stop at the grain. The text lists the vineyards and olive groves right along with it.

The answer is True. After the Philistines burned his wife and her father to death, Samson told them, “Because you have done this, I will not rest until I have taken vengeance upon you” (Judges 15:6-7). That is a heavy moment, friends. I think this is where the story turns very dark.

The answer is cave. After striking down the Philistines, Samson went down and stayed in the cave at the rock of Etam (Judges 15:8). The text doesn't say why he stayed there, so I won't guess. Later, the men of Judah go to that very cave to find him (Judges 15:11).

The answer is arrest. The Philistines say, “We have come to arrest Samson and pay him back for what he has done to us” (Judges 15:10). So the army parks near Lehi and names its reason. And Judah, the tribe being camped on, is stuck in the middle of it.

The answer is that he did to them what they did to him. Samson answers, “I have done to them what they did to me…” (Judges 15:11). The men of Judah had asked, “What have you done to us?” and Samson doesn't dodge. He gives them one short answer. I think he figures it explains itself.

The answer is True. Samson says to the men of Judah, “Swear to me that you will not kill me yourselves” (Judges 15:12). They agree not to kill him, but they will tie him up and hand him over (Judges 15:13). So Samson gets one promise out of them. It's a small deal, but it's a deal.
The answer is two new ropes. They bound him with two new ropes and led him up from the rock (Judges 15:13). Two new ropes, friends. Not one, and the text says new.

The answer is False. The Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him, and the ropes on his arms became like burnt flax. The bonds broke loose from his hands (Judges 15:14). The strength comes from the Spirit of the LORD.

The answer is the fresh jawbone of a donkey. He found the fresh jawbone of a donkey, reached out his hand and took it. Then he struck down a thousand men (Judges 15:15). That's what was lying there, and he took it. I'd have grabbed a rolling pin, friends, so I'm glad nobody asked me.

The answer is that he names it Ramath-lehi. When Samson had finished speaking, he cast the jawbone from his hand. Just before that he said, “With the jawbone of a donkey I have piled them into heaps” (Judges 15:16). Then he named that place Ramath-lehi (Judges 15:17). Speech finished, jawbone dropped, place named. That's a mic drop with paperwork, friends.

The answer is whether he must now die of thirst. Samson cries out, “Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?” (Judges 15:18). He had just struck down a thousand men, and now he's asking about dying of thirst. I think he's worn out, friends. Honestly, I'd be asking the same thing.
The answer is water. God opened up the hollow place in Lehi, and water came out of it (Judges 15:19). Samson cried out, and water came. That's about as plain as an answer gets.

The answer is True. The text says, “When Samson drank, his strength returned, and he was revived” (Judges 15:19). He was worn out and thirsty, and the water changed that. That's the whole turnaround in a single verse.

The answer is twenty years. The text says Samson judged Israel for twenty years in the days of the Philistines (Judges 15:20). A judge is a leader of Israel. Twenty years is a long stretch, friends. And the story isn't over yet.
